title: Long and short: profit both ways
desc: Making money from rises and from falls

cards.added: Opener on the p.13 short-selling idea; $80 → $70 numbers illustrative · Visual: Illustrative chart: tops at $86, rolls over to $80, forecast fall to $70
cards.name: The situation
cards.title: Profit from a fall?
cards.situation: It’s turning down at $80 and you think it will hit $70. You own none. Can you still make money?

chart.label: A stock tops near $86, turns down to $80, with a forecast fall to $70

options.text: Only if I already own the stock
options.feedback: You don’t need to own it. Your broker can lend you shares to sell now and buy back later. The real catch is the risk, which this lesson shows.

options.text: Yes: borrow shares, sell at $80, buy back at $70
options.feedback: Your broker lends you shares. You sell them first, buy them back cheaper later, and return them. The difference is yours.

options.text: No: you only make money when prices rise
options.feedback: Most beginners think this. But you can sell first and buy later. That’s called selling short, and it profits from a fall.

cards.work: Sell borrowed share at $80 − buy it back at $70 = $10 gain a share.

cards.title: That’s going short
cards.text: **[[long|Going long]]** is the normal way: buy, then sell higher. **[[short|Going short]]** flips it: borrow shares from your broker, sell them now, buy them back cheaper and return them. Either way, profit = (sell − buy) × shares.

items.text: Shorting needs a margin account. While you’re short you pay a fee to borrow the shares, margin interest, and any dividend. Many beginner apps don’t allow it.

cards.added: Mirror-image slider interaction · Visual: Price slider drawn at $90: long +$1,000, short −$1,000 on 100 shares from $80
cards.title: Mirror images
cards.text: Drag the price. You’re long 100 shares at $80 and your friend is short 100 at $80. Every dollar you gain, they lose, and the other way around.

cards.added: Worked numbers $40 → $80 → $120 added to the p.14 warning · Visual: Long vs short worst case from $40 (worked numbers added)
cards.title: The nasty twist: no ceiling
cards.text: Buy at $40 and the worst case is $0: you lose $40 a share, 100%. Short at $40 and the price can rise to $80 (−⁠$40) or $120 (−⁠$80) and keep going. In a **[[squeeze|squeeze]]**, heavily shorted stocks have doubled in days.
cards.rule: shorting is for experienced traders, with small size and tight stops.
cards.line: A short can lose more than you put in.

cards.name: Short squeeze
cards.title: The short goes wrong
cards.q: You short 50 shares at $40. The price rises to $46. What’s your result so far?

options.feedback: The size is right, but the sign is wrong. A short wins when the price falls. Here the price rose, so the same amount is a loss.
$46 is the current price, not the result. What counts is how far the price moved from where you sold, times your shares.
You sold first, so you must buy back. The price is now higher than where you sold, so buying back costs more than you got.
Not closing doesn’t stop the loss. If you bought back right now, you’d pay more than you sold for. That loss is real today.

cards.work: Sold at $40 − buy back at $46 = $6 loss a share. $6 loss × 50 shares = $300 loss.

cards.title: Why is shorting riskier?
cards.q: Why can shorting be riskier than buying?

options.text: You can’t use stop-losses on shorts
options.feedback: You can, and you should. A buy stop above your short entry closes it if the price rises (Lesson 1).

options.text: Shorts can only be held for one day
options.feedback: There’s no such rule. You can hold a short for days or longer.

options.text: A short’s potential loss is unlimited
options.feedback: A price can only fall to $0, but it can rise without limit. So a short’s loss has no ceiling.
Shorts do carry extra costs: borrow fees, margin interest and any dividends you owe. But the real danger is the price rising: $40 → $120 loses $80 a share.

cards.headline: You can profit from a fall, and you know the risk.
lines: Short: borrow and sell first, buy back lower.
A short’s loss has no ceiling. Keep the size small and set a stop.
